items.title: 3.3.2 Valence shell electron pair repulsion model (VSEPR)

source_refs.note: Topic 3.3.2, printed pages 52-58 (Table 3.1, Figures 3.9 to 3.20), with Quick Checks 3.5 and 3.6 read in the self-check. No 3.3 or 3.3.1 is printed.

blocks.text: The VSEPR model describes the shapes of molecules from the electron pairs that surround the central atom. It was presented by Sidgwick and Powell in 1940 and rests on the assumption that a molecule takes the shape in which the electronic repulsions among the valence electrons of the central atom are at a minimum. To have minimal repulsions the electron pairs arrange themselves at the farthest possible distances, and this arrangement determines the geometry of the molecule.

items: Both the lone pairs (non-bonded) and the bond pairs take part in determining the geometries of molecules.
The electron pairs are arranged around the central atom so as to stay at maximum distance apart and avoid repulsions.

The electrons of lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs, so non-bonding pairs exert greater repulsive forces on bonding pairs and tend to compress them. The repulsions decrease in the order lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair. An electron pair shared by two nuclei occupies less space than a lone pair bound by a single nucleus.
The two electron pairs of a double bond and the three of a triple bond contain a higher charge density but are regarded as single pairs.
Highly electronegative atoms on the central atom decrease the repulsions between the bond pairs but strengthen the repulsion by the lone pair.

blocks.alt: A strip of two drawings. Left: atom X and atom H with a long, narrow electron cloud stretched between them (a bond pair). Right: atom X with a broad, rounded electron cloud on one side only (a lone pair), visibly fatter than the bond-pair cloud.
blocks.caption: An electron pair shared by two nuclei occupies less space than a lone pair bound by a single nucleus (original drawing after the strip printed above the postulates in the textbook).

blocks.text: The central atom is named A and the electron pairs around it B, giving molecules of the types AB2, AB3, AB4 and so on according to the valency of A. The electron pair geometry is determined by the total number of electron pairs around A, whereas the actual shape of the molecule is determined by the atoms, excluding the lone pairs. The steps are: choose the central atom, usually the least electronegative atom or the element with the fewest atoms (carbon in CCl4); count the electron pairs around it, bond pairs and lone pairs (four bond pairs and no lone pair in CCl4); read the electron pair geometry from the table (four pairs, tetrahedral); then give the shape, excluding any lone pairs.

blocks.caption: Geometries and shapes of covalently bonded compounds (Table 3.1)

blocks.text: In AB2 molecules the two electron pairs lie at 180 degrees, a linear geometry: BeCl2 has beryllium as the central atom with two bond pairs and no lone pair.

blocks.alt: Left: Cl-Be-Cl in a straight line with a curved double arrow over Be labelled 180 degrees. Right: a ball-and-stick model with two large blue Cl balls joined through a small red Be ball in a straight line.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.9: Linear shape of the BeCl2 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.9).

blocks.text: In AB3 molecules three electron pairs lie at 120 degrees, a trigonal geometry: BF3 is trigonal planar with each F-B-F angle 120 degrees, and the hydrides of group 13, AlH3, GaH3 and BH3, are expected to be the same.

blocks.alt: Left: B in the centre bonded to three F atoms, one above and two below, with a curved double arrow between two F atoms labelled 120 degrees. Right: a ball model with a large red B ball and three small blue balls at the corners of a triangle.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.10: BF3 is an AB3 system having triangular planar geometry (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.10).

blocks.text: In SnCl2 the tin atom has four outer electrons; it makes two bonds and keeps the other two as a lone pair which occupies one corner of the triangle, giving a distorted trigonal electron pair geometry in the vapour phase and a v-shaped molecule with an angle under 120 degrees. With multiple bonds, SO3 has all three regions occupied by S=O bonds and is perfectly trigonal at 120 degrees, while SO2 has a lone pair at one corner and a double bond at each of the other two, so it is angular like SnCl2.

blocks.alt: Left: SO3 with S in the centre and three S=O double bonds to O atoms at the corners of a triangle, one angle marked 120 degrees. Right: SO2 with a lone-pair lobe carrying two red dots above S and two S=O bonds below; the O-S-O angle is labelled 'Less than 120 degrees'.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.12: Shapes of multiply bonded SO2 and SO3 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.12).

blocks.text: In AB4 molecules the four electron pairs avoid each other by taking the corners of a regular tetrahedron with bond angles of 109.5 degrees. In methane each of carbon's four valence electrons pairs with the single electron of a hydrogen atom, and the four bond pairs point to the corners of a tetrahedron, a non-planar arrangement; every H-C-H angle is 109.5 degrees, and SiH4, GeH4 and CCl4 have the same shape. A tetrahedron has four corners, four faces, six edges and six bond angles.

blocks.alt: Left: a ball-and-stick model of methane, a black C ball joined to four light-blue H balls at the corners of a tetrahedron outlined in blue. Right: a line drawing of CH4 with C bonded to four H atoms, dashed lines joining the H atoms into a tetrahedron, and the H-C-H angle marked 109.5 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.13: Regular tetrahedral shape of the CH4 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.13).

blocks.text: In ammonia three atoms and one lone pair surround nitrogen; the lone pair reduces the ideal 109.5 degrees to 107 degrees and the molecule is a trigonal pyramid. Replacing hydrogen by electronegative atoms reduces the angle further: in NF3 the angles are compressed to 102.5 degrees, because the strong polarity of the N-F bond lets nitrogen pull the lone pair closer, which repels the bonding electrons more strongly, and because the bond pairs sit nearer the fluorine atoms, which weakens their mutual repulsion.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of NH3. Left: a tetrahedron with N in the centre, three H balls at three corners and a lone-pair lobe with two dots at the top corner. Middle: a ball model of the pyramidal molecule, N above three H atoms. Right: a wedge-and-dash drawing of N with three H atoms, dashed lines joining the H atoms, and an arrow to the H-N-H angle labelled 107 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.14: Distorted geometry and pyramidal shape of the NH3 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.14).

blocks.text: Water is v-shaped with four electron pairs, two of them lone pairs at two corners of the tetrahedron; their greater repulsion reduces the angle to 104.5 degrees.

blocks.alt: Left, labelled 'Tetrahedral geometry including lone pairs': a red O ball in a tetrahedron with two H balls at the lower corners and two lone-pair lobes, each with two dots, pointing up and down. Right, labelled 'Angular shape of water molecule excluding lone pairs': a bent ball model of H2O and a line drawing H-O-H with the angle marked 104.5 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.15: Water molecule has two lone pairs and is v-shaped with suppressed bond angle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.15).

blocks.text: Ions follow the same rules: the hydronium ion H3O+, formed when water captures a proton, is AB4 with one lone pair and is trigonal pyramidal like ammonia; the amide ion NH2- has two lone pairs and two bond pairs, a tetrahedral geometry and a bent (v) shape like water.

blocks.alt: Four parts. 'Hydronium ion': a water molecule with red lone-pair electrons, a curved arrow from a lone pair to H+, and an arrow down to the H3O+ Lewis structure with one lone pair and a + charge. 'Tetrahedral electron pair geometry': O in a tetrahedron with three H balls and a lone-pair lobe at the top. 'Trigonal pyramidal shape': O ball above three H balls. 'V-shaped amide ion': N with two green lone-pair lobes and two bonds to H at 104.1 degrees, in square brackets with a minus charge.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.16: Shapes of hydronium (H3O+) and amide ions (NH2-) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.16).

blocks.text: In AB5 molecules the five electron pairs spread over the corners of a trigonal bipyramid: three positions in a planar triangle and two along an axis perpendicular to the plane, as in PCl5, with angles of 120 degrees within the plane and 90 degrees between an axial and a planar atom.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of PCl5. Left: the Lewis structure, P bonded to five Cl atoms, each Cl with three lone pairs. Middle: five grey electron-pair lobes around a red P ball inside a dotted trigonal bipyramid. Right: a ball-and-stick model with a red P ball and five green Cl balls, two on the vertical axis and three around the middle.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.17: Lewis structure and shape of PCl5 molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.17).

blocks.text: Lone pairs change the shape more dramatically here. The tri-iodide ion I3- is linear although it is an AB5 system: the central iodine has five pairs, two bond pairs and three lone pairs, so its geometry is trigonal bipyramidal; the lone pairs take the three corners of the triangle and the two iodine atoms the apices above and below the plane, and excluding the lone pairs the shape is linear with the iodine atoms 180 degrees apart.

blocks.alt: A red central iodine ball with two iodine balls straight above and below it on a vertical rod, and three grey lone-pair lobes around the middle, one to the left and two to the right. A semicircular arc on the left joins the top and bottom iodine atoms and is labelled 180 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.18: Shape of tri-iodide ion ([I3]-) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.18).

blocks.text: In AB6 molecules six electron pairs take an octahedral geometry, four at the corners of a planar square and two on the perpendicular axis, with all angles 90 degrees, as in SF6.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of SF6. Left: the Lewis structure, S bonded to six F atoms, each F with three lone pairs. Middle: an octahedral ball-and-stick model, a yellow S ball joined to six green F balls with dashed octahedron edges. Right: a wedge-and-dash drawing with F above and below S, two hashed bonds behind and two wedged bonds in front, and two angles marked 90 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.19: Lewis structure and octahedral shape of SF6 with each angle of 90 degrees (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.19).

blocks.text: XeF4 is AB6 with four bond pairs and two lone pairs; the lone pairs stay farthest apart at 180 degrees, and excluding them the shape is square planar with all angles 90 degrees.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of XeF4. Left: the Lewis structure, Xe with two lone pairs bonded to four F atoms, each F with three lone pairs. Middle: an orange Xe ball with four green F balls around it and two blue lone-pair lobes pointing up and down, with an arc and the label 'lone pair is farthest at 180 degrees'. Right: a square planar ball model, Xe in the centre of a dashed square of four F atoms, with one angle marked 90 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.20: Lewis structure and square planar shape of XeF4 (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.20).
